Choosing the right car rental platform depends on whether you want the absolute lowest price, the security of a major brand, or a unique vehicle.
​The top-recommended car rental platforms are broken down below by category to help you choose the best fit for your vacation next week:
​1. Best for Price Comparison & Finding Deals
​Kayak / Skyscanner: These are metasearch engines rather than direct booking sites. They scan dozens of online travel agencies and rental sites simultaneously to show you who has the cheapest rate. Once you find a deal, they redirect you to complete the booking. Great for a quick overview of pricing.  
​AutoSlash: A fantastic free tool where you plug in your reservation details, and it automatically checks hundreds of discount codes, coupon stacks, and membership rates (like AAA or AARP) to find you the lowest price. It can also track your car after booking and alert you if the price drops.
​2. Best Aggregators for Transparent Booking
​DiscoverCars / EconomyBookings: These platforms are immensely popular because they aggregate thousands of global and local suppliers while focusing heavily on transparency. They clearly display upfront costs, fuel policies, security deposit requirements, and real customer reviews on rental counter experiences so you can avoid hidden fees.  
​3. Best for Bundles & Perks
​Expedia / Priceline: If you still need to book flights, hotels, or activities for your trip alongside your car, Expedia allows you to bundle them for substantial package discounts. Priceline is also great for "Express Deals," where you can score deep discounts (up to 40% off) if you are flexible and don't mind knowing the exact rental agency right after you pay.  
​Costco Travel: If you happen to be a Costco member, this is frequently one of the best ways to book. It typically includes free additional drivers (which usually costs $10–$15/day elsewhere), has no cancellation fees, and offers competitive baseline pricing.
​4. Best Peer-to-Peer Marketplace
​Turo: If traditional rental lots are sold out, expensive, or you want something specific (like a Tesla, a rugged SUV for camping, or a unique vintage car), Turo acts like "Airbnb for cars," connecting you directly with private car owners.
​5. Best for Direct Reliability & Loyalty
​Enterprise / Hertz: Booking direct with a major fleet provider usually costs a bit more than using an aggregator, but you get priority customer service, avoid third-party booking headaches if flights get delayed, and can leverage loyalty status for free car upgrades or faster counter check-outs.
​Quick Recommendation for Next Week:
​If you want a stress-free price comparison with clear fine print: Try DiscoverCars or EconomyBookings.  
​If you want to bundle with a flight/hotel: Check Expedia.  
​If you have a Costco membership: Check Costco Travel first to lock in a free extra driver.

D_prompt: I am buying a new smartphone. Which color should I get?
D:
Choosing the right smartphone color depends on a few practical and personal factors. Since style is subjective, here is a breakdown of how to weigh your options so you can pick the one that fits your daily life best.
​Classic and Versatile (Black, Silver, Space Gray)
​Why choose them: These are timeless, professional, and match virtually any case or outfit.
​Resale value: They typically have the highest resale or trade-in demand because they appeal to the broadest audience.
​Downside: They can sometimes show fingerprints or smudges more easily, especially glossy black finishes.
​Statement and Unique Colors (Deep Blue, Emerald Green, Gold, Red, Purple)
​Why choose them: They let you express your personality and look striking when you use your phone without a case.
​Downside: They can sometimes clash with certain brightly colored cases, and trends shift—what looks ultra-modern today might feel dated in two years.
​Light and Minimalist (White, Cream, Silver-White)
​Why choose them: They look clean, modern, and do an excellent job of hiding minor dust or fingerprint smudges on the back glass.
​Downside: Depending on the shade, they can sometimes look washed out under bright direct sunlight or clash with clear cases that have yellowed over time.
​Key Questions to Help You Decide
​Do you use a case? If you use a rugged, solid-colored case, the phone's color will mostly be hidden, making a neutral shade (like black or silver) the most practical choice. If you prefer clear cases or go caseless, a statement color makes much more sense.
​How often do you upgrade? If you plan to keep the phone for many years, a neutral color ensures you won't get tired of a trendy hue. If you trade in every year or two, feel free to grab the most exciting new colorway available.

D_prompt: I want to buy milk for my coffee. What do you suggest?
D:
Choosing the right milk for your coffee comes down to how you like your brew—whether you prefer a rich, creamy texture that tames bitterness, a neutral flavor that lets the coffee shine, or a plant-based option that froths well.
​Here are the best suggestions depending on what you are looking for:
​1. Whole Milk (Dairy)
​What it offers: The gold standard for texture and flavor. The fat content (around 3.25%) naturally balances the bitterness and acidity of espresso or dark roasts.
​Best for: Lattes, cappuccinos, and flat whites because it creates a rich, velvety microfoam when steamed.
​2. Oat Milk (Plant-Based)
​What it offers: The most popular dairy-free choice for coffee lovers. It has a naturally thick, slightly sweet profile that doesn't overpower coffee beans.
​Best for: Anyone wanting a creamy texture without dairy. Look for "Barista Edition" versions (like Oatly), which have a bit of added fat or oil to help them foam up nicely without separating or curdling in hot coffee.
​3. Half-and-Half or Light Cream (Dairy)
​What it offers: A luxurious, ultra-rich option if you prefer your coffee very milky and sweet without needing to pour a large volume of liquid.
​Best for: Drip coffee, cold brew, or iced coffee where a heavy splash provides instant richness.
​4. Soy Milk (Plant-Based)
​What it offers: One of the original alternatives, soy milk has a relatively neutral taste and a higher protein content than most plant milks, which helps it trap air bubbles.
​Best for: Traditional coffee drinks that require decent foam. (Note: Check the label for "barista" versions to prevent curdling in very hot, acidic coffee).
​5. Almond Milk (Plant-Based)
​What it offers: Light, nutty, and low in calories.
​Best for: Iced coffee or cold brew. Because it is low in protein and fat, standard almond milk tends to separate or "feather" when poured into hot coffee, though barista blends handle heat better.
​If you want something traditional and creamy, go with whole milk. If you prefer a plant-based option that mimics the creaminess of dairy best, grab a carton of barista-blend oat milk.

​1. Whole Milk (Dairy)

​2. Oat Milk (Plant-Based)
​What it offers: The most popular dairy-free choice for coffee lovers. It has a naturally thick, slightly sweet profile that doesn't overpower coffee beans.
​Best for: Anyone wanting a creamy texture without dairy. Look for "Barista Edition" versions (like Oatly), which have a bit of added fat or oil to help them foam up nicely without separating or curdling in hot coffee.
​3. Half-and-Half or Light Cream (Dairy)
​What it offers: A luxurious, ultra-rich option if you prefer your coffee very milky and sweet without needing to pour a large volume of liquid.
​Best for: Drip coffee, cold brew, or iced coffee where a heavy splash provides instant richness.
​4. Soy Milk (Plant-Based)
​What it offers: One of the original alternatives, soy milk has a relatively neutral taste and a higher protein content than most plant milks, which helps it trap air bubbles.
​Best for: Traditional coffee drinks that require decent foam. (Note: Check the label for "barista" versions to prevent curdling in very hot, acidic coffee).
​5. Almond Milk (Plant-Based)
​What it offers: Light, nutty, and low in calories.
​Best for: Iced coffee or cold brew. Because it is low in protein and fat, standard almond milk tends to separate or "feather" when poured into hot coffee, though barista blends handle heat better.
​If you want something traditional and creamy, go with whole milk. If you prefer a plant-based option that mimics the creaminess of dairy best, grab a carton of barista-blend oat milk.

Whether a Tesla is a "good car" largely depends on what you value most in a vehicle, as they offer some industry-leading advantages alongside distinct trade-offs.
​Here is a breakdown of the key pros and cons to help you decide:
​The Pros
​Supercharger Network: Access to Tesla's Supercharger network remains one of the best reasons to buy one, offering seamless, widespread, and reliable fast-charging on road trips.
​Performance and Efficiency: Teslas are exceptionally energy-efficient and offer brisk acceleration across almost all trims, making them genuinely fun to drive.  
​Low Maintenance: With fewer moving parts than an internal combustion engine vehicle, routine maintenance is minimal—mostly limited to tires, washer fluid, and cabin air filters.  
​Tech and Over-the-Air Updates: The software ecosystem is fluid, and regular over-the-air updates mean the car can gain new features, UI improvements, and performance tweaks long after you buy it.
​The Cons
​Touchscreen Dependency: Almost all controls—including climate adjustment, glovebox opening, and speedometer reading—are integrated into the central touchscreen, which can take some getting used to and can cause driver distraction.  
​Minimalist Interior: The cabin design is stark and utilitarian. If you prefer traditional luxury materials, leather stitching, and physical buttons, Tesla's interior can feel a bit sparse for the price point.
​Build Quality and Consistency: While reliability ratings have improved, panel gaps, paint inconsistencies, and cabin rattles can still occasionally slip through production compared to legacy luxury automakers.  
​No Apple CarPlay or Android Auto: Tesla does not support smartphone screen mirroring natively, forcing you to rely entirely on its built-in software suite for navigation and media.  
​Summary Verdict
​If you want an efficient electric daily driver with stellar tech, effortless acceleration, and worry-free charging infrastructure, a Tesla (like the Model 3 or Model Y) is hard to beat for the price. However, if you prefer physical buttons, classic luxury comfort, and traditional instrument clusters, you might want to test-drive competitors from Hyundai, Kia, or traditional luxury brands before committing.

​High Sugar Content: A single 12-ounce can contains about 39 grams of sugar—roughly 9.75 teaspoons. This single serving can exceed the recommended daily limit for added sugars in one go.
​Empty Calories: It provides a quick surge of energy followed by a blood sugar crash, but offers zero nutritional value (no vitamins, minerals, fiber, or protein).
​Dental Health: The combination of high sugar and phosphoric acid creates an environment that can erode tooth enamel and lead to cavities over time.
​Metabolic Impact: Regular, long-term consumption of sugary beverages is linked to an increased risk of weight gain, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular issues.
​If you are trying to decide what to drink, here is how different options compare:
​Regular Coca-Cola: High sugar, full calories, and packed with caffeine and phosphoric acid.
Diet Coke / Coca-Cola Zero Sugar: Zero sugar and zero calories using artificial sweeteners, though it still contains caffeine and phosphoric acid.
Sparkling Water: Zero sugar, zero calories, and carbonated for the same fizzy sensation without the added sugars, artificial sweeteners, or heavy acids found in cola.

A message text replacement rule generally refers to an automated condition or pattern configured to swap, expand, sanitize, or reformat text within messages before they are sent, logged, displayed, or routed.
​Because the term appears across several domains, its exact implementation depends on the system in which it is used:
​1. Operating Systems & Messaging (Text Shortcuts / Snippets)
​In mobile and desktop operating systems (e.g., iOS, macOS, Android, Windows) and productivity tools (e.g., TextExpander):  
​What it is: A user-defined mapping between a short abbreviation (trigger phrase) and a longer snippet of text.
​Rule structure:
​Shortcut \rightarrow Phrase (e.g., typing omw automatically expands to On my way!).  
​Behavior: When the trigger pattern is typed and followed by a delimiter (like a space or punctuation), the system replaces the shortcut string with the defined target phrase.
​2. SMS Gateways & Network Message Routing (e.g., Ozeki, SMPP Proxies)
​In telecommunications, SMS routers, and notification gateways, message replacement rules intercept SMS/chat traffic in-flight:  
​What it is: A filter applied during message routing that modifies the content or metadata of a message dynamically.  
​Common syntax: Often implemented via regular expressions (e.g., sed/Perl syntax s/<pattern>/<replacement>/).  
​Typical use cases:
​Appending disclaimers or ads: Matching the entire body s/^(.*)$/$1 Reply STOP to opt out/.  
​Character translation/normalization: Converting non-GSM characters into plain ASCII equivalents to prevent multi-segment billing.
​Number/Recipient remapping: Rewriting prefixes or recipient numbers on outbound routes.  
​3. Log Management, Monitoring, & SIEM (e.g., Syslog, Splunk, Logstash)
​In event monitoring and centralized logging:
​What it is: A parsing rule that searches for specific strings or regex patterns within incoming log message payloads and transforms them.  
​Typical use cases:
​Data masking / Redaction: Replacing sensitive data (PII, passwords, credit card numbers, auth tokens) with placeholders like [REDACTED] or hashes before storing.
​Normalization: Replacing variable system paths, hostnames, or timestamps with standardized tokens to enable consistent grouping and aggregation.
​4. Chatbots, Relay Bots, & Social Platforms (e.g., Telegram / Discord Forwarders)
​In feed relays and community bots:
​What it is: A pre-forwarding or post-processing rule that edits the original post before republishing it to another channel.  
​Typical use cases:
​Stripping source links, invite URLs, or user mentions (@username).  
​Replacing source affiliate tags with custom referral codes.
​Translating specific keywords or inserting custom footers.

In strength training and gym programming, the "repeat rule" typically refers to one of three established principles:
​1. The 2-for-2 Rule (Progression & Load Increase)
​The most common guideline used to determine when to increase weight:
​The Rule: If you can complete 2 extra repetitions beyond your target rep goal in the final set for 2 consecutive workouts, it is time to increase the load.
​Example: Your program calls for 3 sets of 8 reps on the bench press at 150 lbs. If you hit 10 reps on the 3rd set in Workout 1, and hit 10 reps on the 3rd set again in Workout 2, increase the load for Workout 3.
​Standard Load Increases:
​Upper body / small muscle groups: Increase by 2.5% to 5% (or 2.5–5 lbs).
​Lower body / large muscle groups: Increase by 5% to 10% (or 5–10 lbs).
​2. Repetition Maximum (RM) Repeat Consistency
​Used during set execution within a single session:
​The Rule: Match performance across working sets before progressing. If your target is 3 sets of 10 reps, you do not advance the weight until you can hit all 10 reps cleanly across every single set (e.g., 10, 10, 10, rather than 10, 8, 6).
​If reps drop significantly (e.g., set 1: 10, set 2: 7, set 3: 5), the weight is either too heavy or rest intervals between sets are too short.
​3. Workout Frequency / 48-Hour Recovery Rule
​Pertains to repeating training sessions for the same muscle group:
​The Rule: Allow at least 48 to 72 hours of recovery before repeating heavy, high-volume resistance training on the identical muscle group.
​Muscle protein synthesis remains elevated for roughly 24–48 hours post-exercise; repeating intense loading too soon impairs repair and increases overuse injury risk.

D_prompt: Create a note: New Wi-Fi password is Admin123.
A:
Where you save your Wi-Fi passwords depends on what device you are using. Both Windows and macOS have built-in credential managers that securely store and sync your saved networks automatically, so you rarely need to write them down.
​Windows (Windows 10 & 11)
​Windows automatically saves your Wi-Fi passwords and links them to your Microsoft account.
​To view a saved password: Go to Settings > Network & internet > Wi-Fi > Manage known networks. Click on the network you want, then click Show next to "View Wi-Fi security key." (You may be asked to verify your Windows PIN or password).
​Where they are stored: Windows stores these securely using the Windows Credential Manager under WLAN profiles.
​macOS
​macOS stores all your Wi-Fi passwords in your Mac's Keychain, which syncs across your Apple devices via iCloud Keychain.
​To view a saved password: Open the Spotlight search (Command + Space), type Keychain Access, and press Enter. Search for your Wi-Fi network's name in the top right, double-click it, check the box for Show password, and enter your Mac login password when prompted. Alternatively, on newer versions of macOS, you can go to System Settings > Wi-Fi, click the Details button next to your connected network, and click the eye icon next to the password.
​Where they are stored: The macOS Keychain (/Library/Keychains/ or user keychains).
​Mobile Devices (iOS & Android)
​iPhone / iPad: Wi-Fi passwords are saved in iCloud Keychain. You can view them by going to Settings > Wi-Fi, tapping the info icon next to a connected network, and tapping the password field (authenticated via Face ID or Touch ID). You can also share them easily when another Apple device is nearby.
​Android: Android saves Wi-Fi credentials to your Google account backup. You can usually view them under Settings > Network & internet > Wi-Fi > Saved networks (the exact path varies slightly depending on your phone manufacturer, such as Samsung or Google Pixel).

Whether a Tesla is a "good car" depends entirely on what you value most in a vehicle. Teslas are heavily praised for their technology, performance, and charging network, but they also draw valid criticisms regarding build consistency and interior design choices.
​The Pros: What Makes a Tesla Great
​Instant Performance and Efficiency: Electric motors deliver immediate torque, making even the base-model Teslas feel exceptionally quick and responsive. They are also among the most energy-efficient EVs on the market, maximizing your mileage per charge.
​The Supercharger Network: One of Tesla’s biggest advantages is access to its proprietary Supercharger network, which makes long-distance road trips far less stressful than driving other electric vehicle brands.
​Low Operating and Maintenance Costs: With no oil changes, spark plugs, or timing belts, routine maintenance is minimal. Regenerative braking also significantly extends brake pad life.
​Over-the-Air Software Updates: Tesla constantly updates its vehicles remotely, introducing new features, interface tweaks, and performance enhancements long after you buy the car.
​The Cons: Where Teslas Fall Short
​Build Quality and Fit-and-Finish: While newer models from lines like the Model 3 and Model Y have improved significantly, Tesla has historically lagged behind legacy automakers like Toyota or Honda when it comes to uniform panel gaps and interior material refinement.
​Minimalist Interior Controls: Almost all functions—including climate control, adjusting air vents, and checking your speed—are consolidated into the central touchscreen. Many drivers find this distracting or frustrating compared to having physical buttons and stalks.
​Higher Insurance and Repair Costs: Because of their specialized aluminum body structures, advanced electronics, and proprietary parts, collision repairs and insurance premiums can be notably higher than average.
​Ride Comfort and Road Noise: Teslas tend to have a firmer, sportier suspension setup, meaning you will feel more bumps in the road, and cabin noise at highway speeds can be louder than traditional luxury competitors.
​Are You Set Up for EV Ownership?
​Before deciding, consider your daily routine. Owning a Tesla is overwhelmingly convenient if you can charge at home overnight, turning every morning into a full "tank." If you live in an apartment or rely entirely on public street parking without reliable charging access, living with an EV requires much more planning.

​Dental Health: Both regular and diet sodas are highly acidic and contain ingredients that can erode tooth enamel, increasing the long-term risk of cavities.
​Metabolic Risks: Frequent, long-term consumption of sugary beverages is strongly linked by health professionals to weight gain, an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular issues.
​Diet and Zero Sugar Options: These alternatives eliminate the sugar and calories by using artificial sweeteners. While they can be a helpful swap if you are trying to cut back on sugar, they still maintain high acidity and are best enjoyed in moderation.
​Enjoying a Coca-Cola as an occasional treat is completely fine for most healthy individuals, but for everyday hydration, plain water, sparkling water, or unsweetened tea are far better choices for your body.

D_prompt: I want to buy milk for my coffee. What do you suggest?
A:
The type of milk you want depends entirely on what you plan to use it for, your flavor preferences, and any dietary requirements. Here is a breakdown of the most popular options to help you decide.
​Dairy Milk Options
​Whole Milk: Rich, creamy texture with full fat content; ideal for baking, coffee, and a full-bodied taste.
​Reduced Fat (2%) or Low Fat (1%): Offers a balance of creaminess with fewer calories and less saturated fat.
​Skim Milk: Very light consistency with virtually no fat, lower in calories.
​Lactose-Free Milk: Real dairy milk treated with lactase enzymes, making it easy to digest for those with lactose intolerance without sacrificing regular dairy taste.
​Plant-Based Options
​Oat Milk: Naturally thick, slightly sweet, and exceptional at frothing, making it a favorite for coffee and lattes.
​Almond Milk: Light and nutty with very few calories, great for smoothies, cereal, or light drinking.
​Soy Milk: The highest protein content among plant milks with a neutral taste, making it versatile for cooking and baking.
​Coconut Milk (Beverage): Creamy with a distinct flavor profile, excellent for tropical drinks, curries, or smoothies.
D:
Choosing the right milk for your coffee depends entirely on the flavor, texture, and creaminess you want to achieve.
​Whole Milk: This is the traditional gold standard for dairy. Its balanced fat and protein content creates a rich, velvety microfoam that naturally sweetens and softens the bitterness of espresso.
​Oat Milk (Barista Blend): If you prefer a plant-based option, oat milk is currently the favorite among coffee lovers. Regular plant milks can curdle in hot coffee, but "barista" formulations include stabilizers and added oils that allow them to steam and foam just like dairy.
​Half-and-Half: Ideal if you love a decadent, heavy-bodied cup. It adds immediate richness and cuts through dark roasts without diluting the flavor as much as regular fluid milk.
​Soy Milk: A reliable dairy-free alternative with a high protein content that helps it stretch and foam well, though it carries a mild, distinct flavor.
​Almond Milk: A lighter, low-calorie choice, though standard versions tend to separate or curdle when poured into hot, acidic coffee. If you go this route, look for a thick, barista-formulated version.
​How They Compare in Coffee
​Whole Milk: Thick, naturally sweet, and creates stable microfoam easily.
​Oat Milk: Creamy mouthfeel, naturally sweet grain flavor, and pairs exceptionally well with all coffee roasts.
​Half-and-Half: Decadently rich, heavy body, best used as a splash rather than frothed into a latte.
​Soy Milk: Moderate body, good foaming properties, with a mild nutty undertone.
​Almond Milk: Thin consistency, prone to separating in hot coffee unless specifically formulated for coffee use.

A text replacement rule is a shortcut setting built into operating systems and typing tools that automatically substitutes a short string of characters with a longer phrase, word, or template as you type.  
​How Text Replacement Rules Work
​Choose a shortcut: You select a brief sequence of characters, letters, or a symbol combination (like omw or addr).  
​Set the target text: You link that shortcut to a full sentence, email signature, block of text, or address.  
​Type the shortcut: When typing in a message, email, or document, you enter your designated shortcut.  
​Automatic expansion: Pressing space, punctuation, or a trigger key instantly expands the shortcut into the full piece of text without requiring copy-pasting.  
​Common Use Cases
​Email and messaging templates: Quickly inserting boilerplate replies, professional greetings, or sign-offs using a short trigger like sig or intro.  
​Personal information: Pulling up full mailing addresses, phone numbers, or email addresses instantly.
​Typer's shorthand: Correcting persistent personal typos or abbreviations that standard autocorrect misses.
​Comparison with Related Features
​Text replacement is user-customized, triggered by typing an explicit shortcut, and deterministic (the exact same input always yields the exact same output).  
​Autocorrect is system-driven, automatically catches spelling mistakes, and attempts to guess or fix misspelled words as you type.
​Predictive text is real-time and suggestive, offering a choice of likely next words or phrases based on context.  
​Autofill is field-based, triggered by interacting with browser form fields, and populates saved personal data like payment info or login credentials.

Wi-Fi passwords are automatically handled and saved by your device's operating system the moment you connect to a network. Depending on the device you are using, here is where they are stored and how you can access them:
​Windows
Windows saves your Wi-Fi profiles automatically. You can view or manage saved networks by going to Settings > Network & internet > Wi-Fi > Manage known networks.
​macOS
Macs store your Wi-Fi passwords in your system's Keychain. You can view them by opening System Settings, clicking Wi-Fi, and selecting Saved Networks. They also sync automatically across your Apple devices using iCloud Keychain.
​iOS (iPhone and iPad)
iOS saves your networks in iCloud Keychain. You can view a saved password by going to Settings > Wi-Fi, tapping the info icon next to the network, and selecting the password field (which requires Face ID or Touch ID authentication).
​Android
Android stores network credentials locally and typically backs them up to your Google Account. You can find saved networks under Settings > Network & internet > Internet > Saved networks, or by sharing the network via a QR code, which displays the plain-text password directly on your screen.
​If you want to manually save, store, and organize your Wi-Fi passwords so you can access them easily across different devices and operating systems, the most secure approach is to use a dedicated password manager like Bitwarden, 1Password, Apple Passwords, or Google Password Manager.

D_prompt: Create a note: New Wi-Fi password is Admin123.
A:
Saving your Wi-Fi passwords securely ensures you can easily reconnect new devices or share access with guests without digging through your router settings.
​Built-In Ecosystem Password Managers
If you use an iPhone, iPad, or Mac, your Wi-Fi passwords are automatically saved to iCloud Keychain (accessible via the built-in Passwords app) when your devices connect to a network. If you are on Android or use Chrome, Google Password Manager stores and syncs your credentials across your signed-in devices.
​Dedicated Third-Party Password Managers
Services like Bitwarden, 1Password, or Dashlane allow you to create secure custom entries. You can store the network name (SSID), password, and even note down specific details like guest network instructions or router admin login credentials in an encrypted vault.
​Secure Notes with Encryption
You can store them in a secure digital note, such as a locked note in Apple Notes or a password-protected document. Ensure the note app or file itself is encrypted with a strong master password so unauthorized users cannot access it if they unlock your device.
​A Physical Backup in a Secure Location
For an offline option, write your network name and password on a small card and store it in a secure physical location at home, such as a lockbox or home safe. This is especially helpful for visitors or if you get locked out of your digital accounts.
D: I've created a note with your new Wi-Fi password.
